own_list: Any signed-in staff member can delete medical notes or perform other sensitive clinic operations because the clinic API has no role restrictions; misuse or a compromised receptionist account can damage clinical records.

Compromise of either API or an exploitable database-query flaw can use its database admin account to read, alter or destroy records beyond that API's business purpose; the private database network does not limit these granted privileges.

The importer does not authorize the sending lab. A malicious or compromised partner can insert fabricated results into pet records; an unrelated sender could do so too if sender authentication is ineffective (mechanism unknown).

If lab submissions are not bound to the correct pet, order and unique result/version, a lab can target the wrong pet, replay old results or overwrite newer clinical information; those validation and replay controls are unstated.
If the billing service does not enforce caller role and invoice scope on every request, staff can open invoices beyond their authority. Priya's belief is not confirmation of enforcement.

If password guessing, credential reuse or session theft is not controlled, an attacker can take over an owner account and read records or book as that owner. The stated pet-ownership check does not stop abuse of the correct stolen account.
If transport confidentiality is absent on owner, staff, lab, invoice or database paths, a suitably placed observer can read records, invoices or credentials; encryption is unknown, not proven absent.

If effective transport and message integrity are absent, an on-path attacker can change accepted bookings, medical records, lab results or invoices; email delivery also needs appropriate recipient and sender handling.

Without reliable attribution and protected audit records, deletion of medical notes, lab submissions and invoice access may not be traceable to the responsible staff account or sender; auditing is unstated.
If capacity controls are ineffective, request floods or large/expensive lab submissions can exhaust the APIs, importer or shared database, interrupting clinical work; no limits are stated.

If stored owner/lab content is used unsafely in database queries, desktop views or invoice email generation, crafted fields can alter queries or execute in a staff-facing client; parsing and output handling are unstated.

If invoice email addresses or recipient bindings are wrong, stale or attacker-changeable without suitable checks, invoices can be sent to another owner or third party, disclosing billing and pet information.
missing: Database privilege after clinic API compromise: An attacker who compromises the clinic API can use its stated database admin account to read, alter or delete records beyond a single staff operation. Row 20 covers the owner API, not this separate process and database flow. Suggested category: elevation-of-privilege; prerequisite: API compromise. Apply: later.

Result replay/version confusion: If the importer does not validate result identifiers, freshness and permitted version transitions, a malicious or compromised lab can replay an old result or submit a wrong-pet/order association, producing misleading clinical history. Source states no such validation. Keep conditional; cross-pet authorization itself is already row 18. Apply: later.

Invoice misdelivery: If invoice recipient addresses or owner-to-invoice bindings are incorrect or can be changed without suitable checks, billing can send an invoice to the wrong owner or a third party. This differs from spoofed invoice emails and interception in rows 4 and 12; recipient/binding controls are unstated. Apply: later.

Non-lab path tampering: If effective transport integrity and equivalent message-integrity protection are absent, an attacker on an owner-to-API, staff-to-API, service-to-database or billing-to-owner path can alter accepted bookings, medical data or invoices. Row 6 covers only the lab ingress path. Split by concrete existing flow when added; do not assume cleartext or absent integrity. Apply: later.

Untrusted content handling: If owner or lab fields are used unsafely in queries or rendered content, a malicious sender can inject database operations or active content into staff views or invoices. No implementation flaw is established; query construction, parsing and output handling need confirmation. Separate query injection from client-content execution when adding claims. Apply: later.

Expensive accepted results: Even with a modest request count, a large or costly-to-parse lab result may exhaust CPU, memory or storage if size/complexity and execution limits are ineffective. This is a resource-cost threat distinct from the many-result flood in row 16; formats and limits are unknown. Apply: later.

Other confidentiality paths: If confidentiality protection is absent, a suitably placed observer can read records on service-to-database paths or invoices on the receptionist-to-billing path. Rows 9-12 do not cover these existing flows; private network reachability alone does not establish transport confidentiality. Apply: later.

Audit coverage beyond clinic edits and lab attribution: If reliable, protected records of owner bookings and invoice access are absent, abuse through a compromised owner or staff account may be disputed without evidence of the actor or action. Rows 7-8 cover different operations. Audit protection and retention are unstated. Apply: later.
19-vet-clinic-records.notes:
First sitting of the case added in #2268, ruled as CSV in conversation. Row numbers refer to the marks file of the one-round bundle.
The reader opened source.md, model.json, claims/stride.json.
The reader wrote the own list before opening the marks file.

Model ruling on entity:pet-owner: KEEP the internet placement as an explicit schema-required abstraction, not a known location or a statement that the owner device is publicly reachable. Actual network membership remains unknown.
Model ruling on entity:partner-lab: KEEP the internet placement as an explicit abstraction of an external sender using the internet. The lab hosting location and inbound exposure remain unknown.

Row 1 (v6:1228687e379553b1): agree. Agree with the explicit successful-authentication and additional-control conditions; the ownership check does not prevent use of a compromised owner account.
Row 2 (v6:752a70ef3d736d64): reject. Possession of credentials alone does not establish successful sign-in when the mechanism and additional controls are unknown. Make successful authentication explicit. Rewrite as: An attacker who successfully authenticates as a staff account using stolen credentials, defeating any additional sign-in controls, can act in the clinic API with that account's full access, including deleting medical notes. Apply: later.
Row 3 (v6:c19bea01eaf325f6): agree. Authentication is unknown, not known absent; the condition preserves that distinction.
Row 4 (v6:547cfe3ac6045094): agree. A conditional sender-impersonation threat on the stated invoice channel, not evidence that email authenticity controls are absent.
Row 5 (v6:f6fa2715af205c52): reject. The source establishes unconditional acceptance of lab results, but does not establish arbitrary pet targeting. Remove "any pet"; row 18 separately conditions the cross-pet scope risk. Rewrite as: A compromised or mistaken partner lab can cause a false test result to be written into a pet's record, because the importer does not check whether the lab may send the result and writes every result the lab sends. Apply: later.
Row 6 (v6:c9740f5a0865de51): agree. Agree if integrity protection includes both effective transport and equivalent message-level protection, rather than merely encryption.
Row 7 (v6:0df3231d50754d85): agree. Conditional attribution gap; the source does not establish whether auditing exists.
Row 8 (v6:0ab4a8e8cdf052fc): agree. Sender-attribution risk is distinct from whether a result was authorized. Auditing is unknown.
Row 9 (v6:2561653828d20423): agree. Conditional confidentiality risk; unknown encryption is not an assertion of cleartext.
Row 10 (v6:38c144558df4bfad): agree. The clinic network does not by itself protect the path to the cloud API.
Row 11 (v6:ffcf64f20a0c5205): agree. Conditional confidentiality risk on the explicitly internet-carried results.
Row 12 (v6:d315c0d4c1e09227): agree. Agree with "protected" understood as confidentiality protection over the relevant mail path.
Row 13 (v6:812a00112d8b5536): reject. The source names receptionist use but does not say vets and nurses are forbidden to read invoices or do not need them. Condition both the policy restriction and missing enforcement. Rewrite as: If clinic policy restricts particular invoices to certain staff roles and the billing service fails to enforce those restrictions on each request, a signed-in staff member may open invoices their role is not authorized to see. Apply: later.
Row 14 (v6:8be6784760d48e67): agree. Conditional storage-copy disclosure; private database reachability does not establish storage or backup protection.
Row 15 (v6:6b091430af357ba9): agree. Plausible conditional flooding impact; neither absent limits nor actual exhaustion is asserted as a fact.
Row 16 (v6:e9e4a30e64072c7c): reject. The current text describes many writes without stating the availability harm. Make resource exhaustion and interruption explicit, and do not infer unauthenticated acceptance from missing authorization. Rewrite as: If effective rate and resource limits are absent, an attacker able to submit results that the internet-facing importer accepts may send enough results to exhaust importer or records-database capacity, delaying or preventing legitimate result imports or clinical record operations. Apply: later.
Row 17 (v6:5803ab3fcb15f26d): agree. The source explicitly grants every clinic operation to every staff account, including deletion. This is misuse of an existing excessive grant.
Row 18 (v6:8d21d166f3f65de5): agree. The intended pet scope is expressly conditional. Keep separate from row 5 as the authorization-scope finding, not an independent proven exploit.
Row 19 (v6:0e1948065a3cd3ec): agree. Conditional role-enforcement finding. The demonstrated business operation is invoice opening; do not infer unstated billing write/admin endpoints. Shares the cause of row 13 but records the authorization aspect.
Row 20 (v6:11d26505f77467e9): agree. Both APIs use the admin database account; compromise is a prerequisite, not a claim that compromise has occurred.
Row 21 (v6:1a906e3773683707): agree. Agree only within actual write permissions. The importer is known to write results, but arbitrary database-wide rights and additional reachable records are not established.

own_list: A signed-in student can change a submission number to read another student's coursework because the service checks student role but not ownership.
A signed-in student can edit or resubmit another student's work by changing the submission number, corrupting the work used for assessment.
A signed-in teacher can bypass the admin start-page role check by opening an admin page directly and use administrative functions for classes, accounts or final grades.

A compromised coursework service can read or alter all submissions, marks and comments within its database grants, even though grants exclude other tables; table-level least privilege does not enforce per-student ownership.
If the grade exporter actually has broader database grants than read-only, its compromise can alter grades or other permitted data. Dana's unverified belief cannot establish the grant boundary.
If district endpoint authentication or authorization is ineffective, grade exports can be sent to an impostor or grades from an unauthorized sender accepted; neither side's mechanism is stated.
If export transport/message integrity or replay checks are missing, an on-path attacker can alter final grades or replay an older export and cause incorrect district records.
If confidentiality is missing on coursework, administration, database or internet export paths, an on-path observer can read student work, comments, account information or grades.

If school-account or session protections are inadequate, a stolen student, teacher or office account can be used for its permitted operations; sign-in is stated but its mechanism and protections are unknown.

Without protected audit records tying edits, marking, admin changes and exports to accounts and versions, a malicious user can dispute changes and the school may not reconstruct who changed a grade or submission.
If upload size, request rate, concurrency or storage controls are ineffective, large submissions or floods can exhaust coursework processing and the shared database, stopping hand-ins or marking.

If coursework content is rendered or parsed unsafely, a malicious student can target a teacher viewing or marking it, potentially stealing a session or changing assessment data; content handling is unstated.
missing: Coursework service compromise within narrow grants: A compromised coursework service can read or modify submissions, marks and comments allowed by its database account, potentially across students. The stated table restriction limits the blast radius but does not establish row-level isolation. Do not extend this threat to the separate accounts or final-grades tables. Apply: later.

Export endpoint/sender impersonation: If the grade exporter fails to authenticate the intended district endpoint, an attacker may receive the grade export as an impostor. If the district accepts exports without authenticating and authorizing the school sender, forged exports may be accepted. These are conditional endpoint checks, not assumptions about the district hosting network. Apply: later.

Export replay and versioning: If the district does not bind an authenticated grade export to the intended school, period and version or reject obsolete repeats, a replayed older export may replace newer grades. The Friday schedule does not establish freshness or replay protection; row 25 addresses alteration in transit, not unchanged replay. Apply: later.

Submission resource cost: If size, parsing-time, concurrency or storage limits are ineffective, a student can send large or expensive coursework that exhausts service or database resources and prevents legitimate hand-ins or marking. This differs from the request-count flood in row 35; no particular file parser or format is established. Apply: later.

Malicious coursework content: If submitted content is rendered or parsed unsafely when a teacher opens it, a student can cause code or active content to execute in the marking context, potentially exposing a teacher session or changing assessment data. Content processing is unstated, so retain the explicit condition. Apply: later.

Other transport confidentiality paths: If confidentiality protection is absent, an on-path attacker can read work or marks on the teacher-to-coursework path, administration data on staff/teacher-to-admin paths, or data on the coursework/export database connections. Existing disclosure claims cover student ingress, district export and admin database writes, not these paths. Apply: later.

Integrity before district export: If effective transport and equivalent message integrity are absent on coursework, marking, administration or database flows, an on-path attacker can alter accepted submissions, marks, accounts or grades before the export runs. Row 25 covers only the outgoing district path; do not infer that school or cloud network membership supplies integrity. Apply: later.

Marking and export auditability: If protected logs do not bind marking actions and exported grade versions to the responsible account or job, disputed marks or a wrong export may not be attributable or reconstructable. Rows 27-28 concern submission edits and admin grade changes, not teacher marking and export provenance. Apply: later.
20-school-coursework.notes:
First sitting of the case added in #2268, ruled as CSV in conversation. Row numbers refer to the marks file of the one-round bundle.
The reader opened source.md, model.json, claims/stride.json.
The reader wrote the own list before opening the marks file.

Model ruling on entity:district-records-system: KEEP the internet placement as an explicit abstraction of the external recipient reached over the internet. Its hosting network and general public exposure are not established.
Model ruling on boundary:school-office-network: KEEP kind=privilege as the declared assumption about an area reserved for office administration. The source also describes network separation; this classification is not evidence of an effective authorization barrier. Preserve the teacher-to-admin flow and the explicit direct-page bypass.

Row 22 (v6:879aa7a523ca350c): agree. "Obtains an account" is read as successful account/session takeover, not merely learning its identifier.
Row 23 (v6:c125d1f3f69b4493): agree. "Obtains an account" is read as successful account/session takeover; teachers have the stated marking grant.
Row 24 (v6:21ac008999040d2b): agree. Directly supported by missing submission ownership checks and the open/change/resubmit workflow.
Row 25 (v6:3e70bc4a12fa51ce): agree. Agree if integrity protection includes both effective transport and equivalent message protection.
Row 26 (v6:0d8d7c4c8b2fc4b2): agree. The direct-page bypass and admin writes are stated. This is the tampering consequence of the same cause recorded in row 36.
Row 27 (v6:70d2289ee419b3b2): agree. Conditional lack of attribution; no audit absence is asserted as fact.
Row 28 (v6:7551bf4b71571763): agree. Conditional audit consequence of the stated admin bypass.
Row 29 (v6:39526945c9d6062c): agree. The source explicitly includes opening work and omits the ownership check. Distinct disclosure consequence from row 24.
Row 30 (v6:5350872b2fd49c75): reject. The source does not establish that all final grades and account information are visible only to office staff, nor exactly what an admin page displays. Condition the forbidden data and its disclosure through the page. Rewrite as: If an admin page exposes account information or final grades that a teacher is not authorized to read, the teacher can obtain that information by opening the page's address directly, because the admin console checks the administrator role only on its start page. Apply: later.
Row 31 (v6:d81cddd504671924): agree. Conditional confidentiality risk on student submissions.
Row 32 (v6:aaf01b7d27a5bd2c): agree. Agree for grades carried in an observed export; observing one path does not imply access to every historical export.
Row 33 (v6:ddcb8a25031880c9): agree. The office-network to cloud-database path is modeled and carries the stated data; encryption is unknown.
Row 34 (v6:f2954f2a8d7fb8bb): agree. Conditional storage-copy disclosure; no assertion that storage access is currently unrestricted.
Row 35 (v6:cd32212e03a90496): agree. Conditional flooding threat against the public submission service.
Row 36 (v6:c271e329ce0fdfb3): agree. Directly supported administrative authorization bypass. Same root cause as rows 26 and 30, with the privilege aspect rather than another independent weakness.
Row 37 (v6:6acac1cce1ca8f35): agree. Explicit missing object check. Same root cause as rows 24 and 29; retain as the authorization aspect rather than count three independent flaws.
Row 38 (v6:de4242a2027cbf21): reject. The source does not say teachers are restricted to their own classes. Add that policy precondition; role-only marking is not automatically an excessive grant. Rewrite as: If teachers are authorized to mark only students in their assigned classes, but the coursework service enforces only the teacher role and not that class scope, a teacher may mark work outside their assigned classes. Apply: later.
Row 39 (v6:0a855e7a0b020c93): reject. Actual permissions may be read-only. Database reach alone does not permit modification; explicitly condition modification on write grants. Rewrite as: If the grade export's database account has write permissions, an attacker who compromises the grade export may alter grades or other records within those write permissions. Whether the account is read-only is unconfirmed. Apply: later.
